claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution.
Components inside a Pulumi package inherit the package's version.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository.
A source-based package's version is the Git tag on its repository.
Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow, typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
Publishing a source-based package involves applying a semver Git tag (for example, `v1.2.3`) to the repository.
Running `pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds such as npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, or the Go module proxy.
An executable-based package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Releases of executable-based packages are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both the source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
Pulumi recommends that a repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type.

A repository containing multiple packages either has to release them in lockstep, forcing unrelated work to share a version, or must invent per-package release tooling that fights how Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are supported and expected, shipping together at the package's version.

Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping a cohesive set of components together inside that package, and using multiple repositories — one per package — to manage the distinct packages an organization publishes.
The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with the supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The Amazon EKS package is available in the Pulumi Registry at https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/.
A repository can define a single Pulumi package via one `PulumiPlugin.yaml` file at the repository root, with components living alongside it in a `components/` directory.
Pulumi does not recommend bundling all of an organization's components into a single giant monorepo package, because doing so forfeits meaningful semantic versioning.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way regardless of whether each component actually changed, which violates semver.
In the worked example, the package is initially released at v1.0.0 with both ComponentA and ComponentB at v1.0.0.
In the worked example, an enhancement to ComponentA causes the package to be released at v1.1.0 even though ComponentB is unchanged.
In the worked example, a breaking change to ComponentB causes the package to be released at v2.0.0 even though ComponentA had no change at all.
